segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Haw, we’re going to get started now. We're glad you came to visit us today.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I'm glad, too, that I'm doing this.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's good, that's good. The reason we're doing this is to record for the kids and adults who go to school here.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That's good. When I came back from living in North Carolina, when I first came back, they told me they were teaching the kids to talk Cherokee. The first time I came here at that time. If you all wanted a speaker, I would. I wanted to help. You know. But nobody called me. This lady told me they speak Cherokee in that house right there. I told her OK, all of them were talking Cherokee. I felt good inside, like my grandpa and grandma. It felt good to see the children talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're learning really good.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, I'm thankful that you all are doing that. I almost lost it, I felt sad when I came back. The kids talking and the elders gathering, talking and laughing. As I'm watching them, I thought, “I'm going to learn it.” As I'm hearing it, the elders talking and the kids talking, I'm learning it. Sometimes I misspeak when I'm saying words. They ask me if I've become a white person.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what they will say.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: The elders say, “You grew up here and you don't talk right.” They didn't understand me when I lived there. Nobody there talks Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's why you forgot.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, I almost forgot it, but I'm saying I'm learning from the elders talking. I'm learning now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You need to hang around with them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That's true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you forget, as you stay around them, you can start understanding it.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I forgot how I would sing the Cherokee songs when I was little. The Cherokees sing at the Piney Creek towards Sallisaw. Their songs are beautiful.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who is the pastor there now?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I don't know who it is, but Dee Byrd goes there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I haven't seen him a long time. Probably about forty years since I've seen him.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: He's still the same, so nice.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Now, I was talking about the video of you talking. You can ask for it if you want to listen to it. Like your grandkids and kids or anybody. They just have to ask for it and they will give it to them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, I was telling the girls, kids, that I was going to do this. They were laughing about it. They told me I was going to get scared. No, if they're talking Cherokee, I won’t get scared. But it's good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The ones sitting here went to school here and graduated. Now they're working here and doing this.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That's good, you all are doing good. Oh, I was going to tell this to the boy when you first came in there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Stan?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That one, the first time I came, he said siyo really good. He was talking good. Then he messed up. I talked good Cherokee to him, and he just looked at me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You scared him.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: He messed up, we thought it was funny. He said the people you are looking for are in there. Then he started talkin’ good again. The second time I came back, he was talking good. I didn't scare him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That one talks good.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, I told him he's doing good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Tell us your English name?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: My name is Katie Livers.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Now in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Gayoida Amuwela is what I say. My dad’s name was Joe Martin Waters and my mom was Inez Livers. In Cherokee, it was Ganoi Uwela. When I was born, nobody signed my birth certificate. That's why I say Waters and Livers when I'm doing this. I liked my dad, but he wasn't around. It was just my mom. Sometimes he would come by.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You would be glad when he would show up.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh yeah, I loved that man. That's why, when the Cherokees are doing something, I want that last name. That's why I say Katie Waters Livers. When I first got my CDIB card, it had it full. When I went back one time, they made a different card and it had half. I said, "What!" I really got mad. “What do you mean by this? The other white card said I was full Cherokee,” I told them. They said, because your dad didn't sign the birth certificate. I told them OK. I wanted the last name, too, but they told me no, just Livers.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's because he didn't sign the birth certificate, right? Did he ever do it?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: No. When I was 21, my dad passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Were you the only child?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh no, my dad had three girls with another wife and two boys. As for Mama, she had two boys and three girls.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There were a lot of you. Were all of you close by?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: No, not really. I would see my dad, not the kids. About 20 years ago, my dad had a heart attack. Since then, we were always talking. At first I didn't know them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So you all still talk to each other.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's good. Where were you born?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah, but I grew up in Stilwell.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Grew up there?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Uh-huh. My grandpa and grandma had land there. I wanted them to help me with a house, but my aunt told me no. Nobody has touched it since my mom, dad, and grandma died.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is it restricted or not?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I don't know. I'm just going to let it go. One aunt is left, Mom’s sister. Yeah there’s only one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Does she live close?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Where they call Dahlognah and Cherry Tree.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My sister works at the school.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Who's your sister?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Her name is Marie Eubanks. She teaches Cherokee there.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, that's where I went to school.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh really? I went to Greasy.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: If you don't mind, how old are you?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: We must have played basketball?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We really played hard. Right?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We really played hard without knowing.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: When you said that Eubanks, that reminded of a Eubanks girl that I played basketball with a long time ago. We used to be Kimble. It was at Cave Springs. There were Eubanks.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I went to school there. Did you go to school there?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I did, too.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Do you know Janet Fourkiller? She's still a nice woman.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I haven't seen her in a long time.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Still the same, nice. She is substituting at Cave Springs.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you graduate there at Cave Springs, not so?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: No I finished in Eufaula. I was cooking at Cave Springs. I quit in January. My nerve was messing up. I had trouble.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Grabbing things.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, and my feet, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What we’re talking about is when you first started school. How old were you?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I was six.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Were you talking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, always. We were always talking Cherokee. My mom didn't talk good English. It was always Cherokee. My grandpa, well, Grandpa talked English.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What were their names?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Taylor Livers Gatogi Uwela, they would say. Ella Mae Seabolt is my granny, Els Uwela. You know, cause she married Grandpa. Yeah, Els Uwela.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How old were you when you started English and learned it? Did you already know how?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Levi Sunday and Grace were their names. They lived close to us. They - how would you say it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They took care of you?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: They taught me how.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They taught you how. I knew Levi.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh yeah, they were nice. I thought that was my grandpa, that old man. I grew up calling him Dudu, and Grace Granny. Where they lived, chickens, horses, dogs, and ducks - what were they called? Oh shoot. They had rabbits, too. I grew up good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were helping with everything there, feeding?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: They had cows, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember those old people.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Cory, that was Gracie’s friend. I was scared of him when I was little. Oh, yeah, I grew up good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You said you went to Dahlongah school. Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, I finished there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were playing ball there.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Did you know Dennis Gonzales?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was related to me that one.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My mother was a Gonzales.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That was my grandpa. That was on the Livers side, that Dennis.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There were a lot of preachers. Some of them were related or kin to my mom.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: The Goodriches.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There's a lot of them, Goodriches.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: We're all related, right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It seems that way.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: You couldn't even find a boyfriend, and they would say that one is kin to you.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's true, they would run him off.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That was true, it was good, right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was good at that time.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: What about Polly Vann? Did you know her?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I knew all of them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Those Proctors living there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Woodrow and all of them, they're related to me, too. All of them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Little John Sams, he’s kin to you, too, right? They're kin to me, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It sounds like we're related.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, oh, really. Little John Sams’ sister is the Proctor.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Their mom and my grandpa were brother and sister. Senora Gonzales, did you know him? They called him Snow. That was my grandpa.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I do, lanky tall man, right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess when he was a young man. I do know, as we get old, we get short. As we get older, we get shorter.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, that's true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His son’s name was Senora, too. They passed a long time back, about 30 years.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I left at that time. I've forgotten a lot of people.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you finished at Dahlonegah, where did you go to school from there?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I went to Cave Springs. From 10th grade, I went to Eufaula.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's why. You had already left when I got there. That's why I didn't know you. When you finished there, how long did you live there?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: When I finished, I came back to Stilwell. Then I got married.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That must have not been good. She's making a lot of faces talking about it.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I have three girls.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do they talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: No, North Carolina.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They live there? Do you have grandkids?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: A lot. Let's see, altogether I have five girls, and two of them live here. What do they call it? River Tree River or something? The Muskogee hospital.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, Three Rivers?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Three Rivers, that’s where one of the girl works. My granddaughter works there in pediatrics. The other one had a baby. She's not working now. She was working at the juice plant at Ft Gibson.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you were growing up, did you have a lot of toys to play with? Did you make them yourself?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: We didn't have a lot to play with. We were always playing on the hill. What was his name, Walkingstick? An old man. He had horses on the hill.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were white people, weren't they?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, they were white people.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I know who you're talking about but I forgot the first names.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, it was Walkingstick, he had horses. My cousin – how would you say ride?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dakiludihe.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That old man was mad because we were there every day and all day.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He didn't want you there.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: He also had pigs, and it was good. We would help him. I grew up always working. My mom was always saying, “If you want to eat, you need to work.” When we help with the pigs, they would give Mom some meat. And Levi with a cow, it was the same, too. They would give her the meat for helping.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you have fun doing that? It was hard work.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: It was. Mommy was always cutting her own wood. We helped her. We worked really hard. We thought it was funny, my mom was funny. Then we would eat biscuits, potatoes, eggs, and bread.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did she have an old wood cook stove? Did she use that? That's really good on that.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: We ate good. I was asking my sister, “When you think about Mom, what are you thinking?” She said, “Her cooking. She was always singing in Cherokee.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She enjoyed cooking, didn't she?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, we didn't have anything. We didn't have anything. A bed. But Levi Sunday brought a TV, our first TV Levi brought, and Mommy got mad. Mom told him to take it back. He said to Mom, “The kids might want to watch cartoons.” She told him no. But, it didn't leave, it was just there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was just sitting there.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: It was a big box, when we first plugged it in. Oh, I'm telling you, we enjoyed it! Then Mommy started watching Lawrence Welk.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what I like. I still like that.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh, no, she started watching TV! At first, she told him she didn't want it because she has good kids, she told him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did he ever come get it?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You all kept it.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yep, Mommy bought another one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She bought a new one.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yep, she bought another one, the box kind. It was good. This one was little.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was black and white. Right?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: But it was good. We would laugh at Jackie Gleason.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Jackie Gleason? Do you all know what that is?
I don't think so.
I think so.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The man was hateful and crazy.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: And Ralph, too. It was good. I tell the kids, “We didn't have nothing, you know.” “What did you do without a phone?” I told her we played, I was still playing with dolls at 13 years old. Not now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We were like that back then. We like to do that.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, kids don't play anymore.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They would run us outside. At night we would run outside. They would say, “Be careful, a skili can join you.” We would come back in scared.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: We knew that, didn't we? Kids are different these days. At one o'clock, the kids were playing at the playground.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some of them do dangerous stuff.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I feel sorry for them. Sometimes I'll come to the house hungry. I cooked at Cave Springs sometimes. When I would make something, I would take it home. I would feed the kids. I feel sad for those kids, they don't know where their parents are at, they have no food.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's sad, ain't it?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Sometimes the church feeds the kids in the summertime. I don't want to move now, there's a lot that goes on there. The kids I feel sorry for, they don't know where their dad and mom are. If you ask where your mom is, they say, “I don't know. She went to the store, I think.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're just by themselves.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: True, I feel sorry for them, but they're soo mean, yeah, mean kids. If you're feeding them, it's good. They ask if I want my trash in the dumpster sometimes. They'll come, but the others - how would you say it? The neighbor doesn't like the kids. Oh, they torture him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They know he doesn't like them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, they don't like that old man.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: As you were talking, when you finished, where did you work? Your first work or did you go back to school?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Huh-uh. At the Stilwell factory is where I worked, the first place I worked for four years.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What did you do there? Nothing?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Everything. Conveyor belt, feeding the machine, everything. When I moved to North Carolina and left, it was in the '90s. I worked good there as a highway maintenance for the city. Graham transportation. I worked there as a heavy equipment operator. I have certificates. I did highway maintenance, like I was telling you, and I raised five girls. Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She said, "YEAH!" You have to pay for the girls. The girls are more expensive, aren't they?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That's true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Clothes.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Let me see, from 1996 to 2009, I worked there. I worked at highway maintenance. I really liked it, and at the tree service. I've done everything, big trucks and equipment. Then I weeded, and those tractors that mow on the side of the road, I've done that, too. My girls are hard workers.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They learned from you, didn't they?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: They're really good workers. The little one works for UPS. When I quit working for ODOT, I worked at the warehouse. Shipping and receiving. At that time, the kids helped me after school. When they would come down, they would help me. They know how to work.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's good, you taught them good. Which job did you like the best?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Heavy equipment.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was it hard to learn it, or not?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I have a certificate for that. I can drive a dump truck for that. I can use a jackhammer. I was a little bigger then.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were really strong back then.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, everything and asphalt I've done, I have certificates to show everything I've done.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: For the schooling.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: The only thing is the grader - too much.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Be driving that.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I like the little one, where you can just put that up: rrrrr and kinda just...

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You have really worked hard.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh yeah, long hours.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you say you were still working at Cave Springs or not?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Not now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I forgot.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I had surgery. They fixed three discs. My nerve was really bothering me. That's why I don't work anymore.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You just retired. Where was your surgery?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Tahlequah, they call it the City there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is it good now?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, it's good, it's good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were talking about helping with the pigs. Did you all have a garden?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: All of us, you knew Levi Sunday, he had all the corn. We helped him, yeah, we always help him, that Levi.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you all can?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: All of us, how do you say tomatoes?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: damatla.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: damatla, a lot of those, a basket full.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So you were canning that. How did you can those?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I can't say it. How do you say ‘peeling them’?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: detsinagali.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were boiling them first and then peeling them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, detsinagali. See, I still mess up.
That's OK, you still talk good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh, you're doing good. I mess up, too, sometimes. This one, too. Not really, just saying that. Just saying that.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: When I'm talking to a Cherokee speaker, I say, “What is it?” And they always look at me and say, “What?”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You all were canning all that, cucumbers, too. The sour or sweet.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Beans, green beans.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I like those with potatoes.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Really, the little ones. I forgot that was noonah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Those were hard to take out. Potato, you had to work hard. Dad had a house this big [gesture]. When we would get them out, we would put them in there. It would get full, he planted that many.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Grandpa had a cellar you had to walk down.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was cold, right, and dark. Plus, they would hang the meat. Was he doing that in the cellar? Cow meat, too, or just pig?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Just pig, I think.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They would cut it when they needed.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: We would see him early in the morning. At that time, a long time ago, women used to know how to cook.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: True, Granny would get up early in the morning to cook. As soon as she finished, she would start lunch.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That's true. Mom, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Bread. She had a bread pan this big [gesture] and another one. Three times a day. I'm the helper, saying I can't do it.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: A long time ago, we all ate together.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was nice, people were always coming to eat.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: True.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember when someone would show up, my grandpa would tell Granny, “Go set the table.” I don't know how many times a day she set the table. People were always eating. She always had food.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: My mom would always cook when someone came. She would feed them before they left.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what they used to do. If it were me, I would give up. Every so often I put food on the table. We’re not like that.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: There's bologna.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I would say, “Go eat bologna.” They were really friendly at that time.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: True.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We used to sleep outside, you probably did, too.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Uh-huh, it was good, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We would talk about skilis, scaring each other. Have you ever experienced skilis?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Ahh, just medicine. My mom always made it. We didn't go to the doctor. My mom used root, onion, honey, garlic, and lemon. Let me see, what else? Anyway, she always used it. We would drink it, I guess for our immune system. We never went to the doctor. Also, the root. I forgot what it was called.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were chewing it?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, it was good. Our teeth were good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Your mom did that? She knew how?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, a lot of people came to the house. Also, the medicine Mommy used was good. Nothing. She didn't ask for money from the people. She didn't do that. She would just help them. I would ask her why. Sometimes she would say, “It's OK.” I would tell her we don't have bread. She would tell me, “Go make biscuits.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Sometimes they would give you food, didn't they?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That was good, but Mom wouldn't take money.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don't know if that kind are still alive. That know-how. Right?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I've taught the kids what I've learned. I know a little medicine. For that mucus if you want it, honey and garlic, mash it with lime and drink it good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's for mucus or what?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, do it for one week, all of it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It will clean it out? Do you drink it, eat it or what?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: As for me, I mash it. One clove or half a clove, a tablespoon of honey, then lime. Mix all of it and drink it. It's good. Do it for one week. Then you will breathe good. Yeah, it's for the respiratory system. They told me I had problems with that. My aunt asked me, “Didn't your mom teach you medicine?” At that time, she told me, there were no inhalers or blood pressure medicine.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You don't take them now.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I don't take them anymore. I still have blood pressure, and breathing – it was improving at that time me and my aunt talked. She told me to do this, and I did it. I don't take high blood pressure now. What they call cholesterol, I don't get those either. What else, I don't take anything, inhaler, too. I got well. Now, when I talk to my aunt, I always ask her to teach me, because I forget.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do you have sugar (diabetes)?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: That's what I mean, what I was telling. You can make your own medicine to help yourself.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I'm going to learn what you're saying. I'm going to try it.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: It's really good, you know yourself. Try it. Do it every day. Eat whole beets for blood pressure. Now, every time I go to the doctor, my blood pressure is 123 over 67. It's just...

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Not high.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: But try this. It will help diabetes. I think it's thyme and ginger will help you if you have diabetes. You don't want to eat a lot of ginger. It's really hot, that’s why you use honey.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's strong, isn't it?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Then put lime in it. You will know if you're a diabetic.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I buy that ginger at the dollar store.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Oh, I'm talking about the root.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I buy those to help my stomach. They're strong.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: It's good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I need to use the root. It would be better.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, really. Worms, if you got worms in your stomach. That, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're making a sound.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: If you get ginger and just eat it, that would help. Long time ago, they used to say, “When you're itching in the back, when you have to scratch,” they said, “you have worms.” A long time ago, that's how you knew you had worms. That's how they find out if the kids have worms in the stomach.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Scratching.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: After that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were coming out. It was killing them.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: You'll have a good diarrhea. Any time you have stomach problems, use ginger and garlic. It will be good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I like garlic.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I do, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about the little people?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yes, they did tell us about it. When we were little, we would hear something when we would play. They would say it was the little people. I've heard them talking and playing. One time we were at the creek, one of them, Brenda, she said, “There's somebody swimming!” she would say. And I would tell her, “No, look, be still!” We got still. They were really swimming, but I didn't see anything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Making noise.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, playing in the water. We could hear them. Boy, we never went back. When we left, we left. We never went back again till this day.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It scared you? Well, we're finishing up now. It went by fast, didn't it?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What do you think about us speaking Cherokee? Do you think it will end?

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, that's why I'm doing this. I want my grandkids to learn. If something happens, that's the only language we're going to have. That's the only way we're going to stick together is our language. Like I was telling you, I almost lost it. Boy, I felt bad. When I came back, I started talking good, I felt good, and I found myself.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You can really talk good.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Thank you. I felt lost ‘cause the elders were saying, “Are you white now?” I got tired of them saying that. I said no, and started listening. The elders would be laughing while we were eating. I would sit there, and they would say, “Do you hear us?” Now I'm talking good, they don't say, “Are you white?” anymore. But I want you all to continue this. If you all need my help for something, I will help.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Thank you.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I'm here, and I enjoyed this.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me too. We're glad you came. Listening to you talk was good.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: I thought I was going to mess up. I was thinking, “What if I freeze up?”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We're nice.

segments.speaker: katie-livers
segments.translation: Yeah, you guys made me feel very comfortable.
